captions:
Let's use these ideas to catch something
surprising
about your own language.
Shannon ran a famous little experiment,
and you can run it in your head
right now.
Take an ordinary English sentence,
cover up the next letter,
and try to guess it before you look.
The quick brown f...
You already know it is an o,
then an x.
You barely had to think.
That is the game,
and in English you win it astonishingly often.
After a q,
you know a u is coming.
At the end of many words,
you can feel the letters before you read
them.
Now connect that to entropy.
A letter looked at completely alone carries about
four point two bits,
as we just computed.
But a letter seen in the context of
everything before it?
Once you have the sentence so far,
the next letter is often nearly certain —
so it carries far less new information.
Watch the meter fall as context builds —
from four point two bits,
down toward roughly one bit per letter,
and by some estimates even less.
Which leads to a striking headline.

Written English is about seventy-five percent
redundant.
Three out of every four letters,
in a sense,
you could have guessed from the rest.
And that redundancy is not a flaw.
It is a feature,
working two jobs at once.
It is exactly what lets you read straight

through typos and autocorrect disasters without
slowing down.
And it is exactly what a compression program
hunts down and deletes.

Redundancy is predictable structure — and
predictable structure
is entropy you are not using.
